articles.title: Seattle’s KEXP eyes a second physical home — in San Francisco’s historic Haight-Ashbury
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Seattle independent radio station KEXP is exploring the possibility of building out a second physical home — far from its beloved base at Seattle Center — in San Francisco.

Three years after expanding its broadcast footprint to the Bay Area with the acquisition of 92.7 KREV FM, the non-profit music institution has set its sights on the city’s historic Haight-Ashbury neighborhood for a potential site.

Under a proposed partnership announced Thursday by KEXP and city preservation group SF Heritage , the station would team up with local nonprofit Blue Bear School of Music to convert the historic Doolan-Larson House and Storefronts at the corner of Haight and Ashbury streets into a multifaceted music and cultural center.

The early-stage plan for the landmark property envisions radio broadcast facilities, a roof venue for live performances and community events, space for group and individual music lessons, and a public “third space” intended for year-round daily gathering.

The proposed hub adds another twist to the long-standing cross-pollination between the two tech capitals. While Silicon Valley giants have routinely set up major engineering outposts in Seattle, and founders and workers migrate between the regions, KEXP’s expansion represents a rare cultural export heading in the opposite direction.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie cheered the proposal as a win for both the neighborhood and the city’s broader economic recovery.

“Art and music have been part of what makes San Francisco special for generations,” Lurie said in a statement. “Innovative partnerships like this one help us reimagine what’s possible and find new ways to activate our neighborhoods. Our artists and cultural spaces make our city stronger, and this new home for music and culture at Haight and Ashbury will inspire generations to come.”

Located at the epicenter of the 1960s counterculture movement, the Colonial Revival-style Doolan-Larson House was originally constructed in 1903 and raised after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake to add ground-floor storefronts.

The property — designated San Francisco Landmark No. 253 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places — housed groundbreaking hippie-era boutiques during the Summer of Love. It was gifted to SF Heritage in 2017 by its long-time owner, the late Norman Larson, specifically to ensure the landmark would be preserved and activated for public and cultural use.

Founded in 1972 as KCMU — a small, student-run station at the University of Washington — KEXP has spent over five decades building a global reputation for human-curated music discovery, famously becoming one of the first stations to champion the “Seattle sound” in the late 1980s.

The station’s Bay Area presence officially materialized in late 2023 when KEXP placed the winning $3.75 million bid at a bankruptcy auction to acquire commercial frequency 92.7 KREV FM (now KEXC). Funded by a portion of a $10 million bequest left by a anonymous long-time donor, the station began retransmitting its broadcast signal to Northern California in March 2024 as part of a strategy to ground its growing digital and streaming audience in key cultural markets.

In Seattle, KEXP’s physical hub at Seattle Center — itself a civic landmark — features a public Gathering Space that combines a coffee shop, record store, and live performance venue alongside its open-view DJ booth.

Translating a high-touch, human-centered physical experience into new markets is a core priority for the station: KEXP recently hired its first chief product and technology officer, former SiriusXM and Nordstrom executive Jyoti Shukla, to build digital products and physical spaces that intentionally prioritize human music curation over AI algorithms.

In a post on LinkedIn , KEXP CEO Ethan Raup said the response to the station’s arrival in the Bay Area “has been nothing short of remarkable” and that it gave KEXP “the confidence to start planning for our next big step.”

In its post on Thursday, KEXP stressed the plans are “not a done deal yet.” Over the coming months, SF Heritage, KEXP, and Blue Bear School of Music will focus on gathering community feedback, finalizing an adaptive reuse plan, and determining construction feasibility and project financing.
KEXP and Blue Bear representatives will make their first public outreach push at the Haight Ashbury Street Fair on Sunday to share more about the proposed project.

articles.title: Startup Ravel raises $8.2M to help solve clothing recycling’s spandex problem
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle startup Ravel announced Thursday it raised $8.2 million to scale its planet-friendly technology for recycling clothing by unwinding the components of synthetic fabric blends.

Ravel has targeted the textile fiber known as elastane , which is also called spandex or Lycra. It’s added to athletic wear, jackets, jeans, underwear, socks, t-shirts, gloves and every other category of apparel. Even in small amounts, elastane makes clothing difficult to recycle.

Ravel has developed a technology for unblending fabrics that include elastane. It turns the recovered ingredient into cost-competitive, recycled plastic pellets that serve as the raw material for making polyester fabrics.
The startup calls its process “purification recycling” and emphasizes that it is energy efficient, uses safe chemicals and does not create added waste or byproducts.

“Even though most of us don’t see it regularly, the ‘behind the scenes’ of materials recovery and valorization is a massive undertaking (and thus massive opportunity),” Ravel CEO Zahlen Titcomb said on LinkedIn .
The investment allows Ravel to transition from its Seattle pilot plant toward commercial-scale operations. It also helps the business validate its solution at production scale with textile partners.

Much of the clothing that is collected for recycling today is downcycled into lower-value uses rather than spun back into new apparel. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation has estimated that less than 1% of material used to make clothing is ultimately recycled into new clothing.
As fast fashion accelerates, apparel brands today are making about twice the amount of clothes that were produced in the early 2000s.
Ravel announced in March 2025 that it had raised pre-seed funding, but did not say how much. The company was a finalist for the Sustainable Innovation Award at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

The seed round was led by One Small Planet with “significant participation” from AP Ventures. Other backers included Overlay Capital and Lichen Ventures, plus existing investors At One Ventures, Collateral Good and BetterWay.
“I’m excited to have found some great folks to roll up the sleeves with,” Titcomb said.

articles.title: Startup Spotlight: Local Crew uses video and AI to cut out in-person home repair estimates
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Saad Nadeem doesn’t have any professional background in home improvement. But like any self-respecting weekend warrior, his experiences as a homeowner have taught him some valuable lessons.
The biggest lesson, perhaps, was to create his own startup to solve his problems.

Nadeem is co-founder and CEO of Local Crew , a newly launched Seattle startup designed to make it easier to find laborers, assess bids, and hire a professional to perform everything from yard work to house repairs.
“Even for straightforward projects, I had to contact several pros, explain the same job repeatedly, arrange on-site visits, and sometimes wait days just to compare estimates,” Nadeem said.
Professionals are equally frustrated, he learned, because traveling to provide free estimates is time consuming, particularly for smaller jobs they may not win.

A Pakistani immigrant and tech veteran, Nadeem has spent nearly a decade working in marketplace operations at companies including Uber, Roblox, and TikTok, focusing on customer experience, support operations, and simplifying complex processes for users.

Local Crew relies on AI to analyze a video submitted by a customer in which a potential job is spotlighted. AI turns the video into a structured job post with a project description, relevant details, and a recommended price. The customer can adjust the price before posting, and local pros can accept it or submit a counteroffer. The main differentiator is Local Crew alleviates the need for multiple calls or in-home estimate visits.
Companies such as Thumbtack, Angi, and Taskrabbit are among the closest small-job and home-improvement comparisons.
Local Crew — now live on iOs and Android — is starting in the Seattle area, with plans to expand into major Midwest cities next and eventually grow nationwide.
“The goal is to prove the model in Seattle, learn from customers and pros, and then expand thoughtfully into additional markets,” Nadeem said.
We caught up with Nadeem for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight to learn more about his startup.
In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch .

Local Crew is a platform that makes it simple for customers to find and hire local professionals for any task. Whether it’s homeowners who need a pro to come fix their leaking faucet, or a student looking for some extra hands to help them move. Local Crew cuts the back and forth and exhausting visits for estimates. Simply record a video of what you need done, and Local Crew analyzes your task, creates a detailed brief, and suggests a price you can set. Local professionals bid on your task and you pick the one that suits you.
What problem are you obsessed with solving?

Hiring someone for tasks is still surprisingly inefficient. Homeowners spend days coordinating visits just to compare quotes, while pros lose hours driving to estimates that never turn into jobs. We’re building a faster, simpler way for both sides to connect.
What surprised you after talking to customers?

We expected homeowners to be our biggest challenge. Instead, we learned that local pros were just as frustrated. Driving across town to provide free estimates for small jobs often wasn’t a good use of their time, especially when many estimates never turned into work. That’s when we realized we were solving a problem for both sides of the marketplace.
How has AI changed the way you build your company?

AI has accelerated everything — from product design and engineering to marketing, customer support, and content creation. It has allowed a small founding team to move with the speed and output of a much larger company.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup? People often assume we’re another lead-generation platform. We’re not. Customers record their project, set the price, and pros bid or counteroffer. The goal is to eliminate unnecessary back-and-forth and quote visits before work begins.
What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Delaying our public launch. We could have launched earlier, but we chose to spend more time improving the experience based on real feedback from early users. It was the harder decision, but the right one.
What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?
Talk to customers far more often than you think you should. The best product decisions usually come from listening, not guessing.
Hiring someone for a home project feels as easy and expected as ordering food or requesting a ride, and homeowners naturally think of Local Crew first.

articles.title: Portland startup Antfly raises $2M to streamline data infrastructure for AI agents
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Antfly , a Portland startup building software to streamline how artificial intelligence systems access corporate data, announced Thursday that it has raised $2 million in pre-seed funding.
The round was led by venture capital firm Heavybit, with participation from 8-Bit Capital.
The company is tackling what developers call the “Retrieval Gap” — the disconnect between the information an AI agent needs to answer a query and what current search systems actually deliver.

When an AI agent handles a complex task, like investigating a customer refund, it must simultaneously search real-time account data, recent policy changes, and old support emails. Today, software teams typically stitch together five or six separate databases and search tools to fetch those scattered records.

Antfly says it replaces that fragmented setup with a single engine and unified API, allowing agents to retrieve grounded, permission-checked data instantly without developers having to maintain a complex pipeline.

Antfly is the third Portland-based startup for CEO and co-founder James McDermott , who previously founded the customer data platform Lytics , which was acquired last year. Drawing on their experience building data platforms at a scale of billions of profiles, McDermott and co-founder AJ Roetker designed Antfly to eliminate the heavy operational burden developers face when building custom retrieval stacks from scratch.

“Every AI team eventually builds the same retrieval stack,” McDermott said in a news release. “Search. Vectors. Graphs. Rerankers. Inference. Memory. Glue code. We don’t think developers actually want six retrieval systems. We think they’re assembling them because the retrieval engine hasn’t existed. That’s what we’re building.”
The practical impact is already playing out for one customer: Visiting Media , a Portland-based immersive sales platform for the hospitality industry.
Before adopting Antfly, CTO Eric Sniff said his team tried building a custom retrieval system in-house, describing the process as “like pushing through mud.”

Using Antfly, a small team of three engineers at Visiting Media indexed more than 100 terabytes of media and text in under 24 hours . That infrastructure now powers an AI agent capable of pulling exact visual and textual assets from their library to build custom digital sales proposals for clients in under a minute .

“None of it was the product we actually wanted to build,” Sniff said of their previous DIY setup. “With Antfly, the team was experimenting within days — trying new indexes and different models. Nobody maintains a retrieval pipeline anymore, and nobody misses it.”

Antfly, which currently employs six engineers working out of a Kiln co-working space Kiln in Southeast Portland, will use the fresh capital to expand its product engineering team and scale support for customers deploying the retrieval engine in production.
The core software is currently available as a free, self-hosted engine for developers to run locally or in private environments, with a fully managed cloud service currently in waitlist status.

articles.title: Seattle's Speed Camera Program Enters New Frontier
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle is set to see four new automatic speed cameras in 2027, but it's not the number of cameras that will make the move notable. The cameras will be the city's first full-time speed cameras, after decades of keeping automatic speed cameras confined to time-limited school zones.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Drivers will encounter the cameras along E Marginal Way S, and Sand Point Way NE, and two different segments of Rainier Avenue S – locations where driver speeds are consistently much higher than posted speed limits. Exact cross-streets where the cameras will be installed are still being determined, according to an announcement from the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT).

SDOT also maintains a constellation of red light cameras, along with less common cameras tasked with enforcing bus-only lanes and intersection blocking. The authority to put up a 24/7 camera away from a school zone comes from a 2024 overhaul to state law governing camera use that was codified into city code last year.

While the issue of the Seattle Police Department's CCTV camera network has been an incredible contentious one during Mayor Katie Wilson's first months in office, a clearer political consensus has emerged around automatic traffic cameras. Unlike CCTV cameras, significant guardrails govern the use of traffic cameras by state law, including the inability for traffic camera footage to be turned over to officers investigating other crimes.

Wilson's executive order accelerating work on traffic safety projects, released on August 21, included a commitment to add 10 cameras to the city's arsenal by early 2029, with these four cameras representing a down payment on that promise.

"Everyone needs to get around safely, and we are committed to our goal of ending deadly crashes and serious injuries in Seattle. As we work to accelerate traffic safety projects throughout the city, we’re moving forward with new 24/7 speed safety cameras in four locations with a history of excessive speeding and deadly crashes," the department wrote in a blog post last week touting the move.

Two of the new cameras – along E Marginal Way and Sand Point Way – will be located along streets that have a posted speed limit that is higher than the city's default arterial limit of 25 mph. But Seattle's 2025 annual traffic report shows that drivers are still regularly exceeding the speed limit there. For example, despite a 30 mph limit along Sand Point Way, the 85th percentile speed – the speed at or below which 85% of drivers travel – was somewhere between 35 to 40 mph.

"Our data shows that 15% of people driving in all four of these locations were traveling 10+ mph over the speed limit," the blog post continued. "Our goal was to boost safety where it’s most needed, while trying to avoid over-concentration of cameras in historically disadvantaged neighborhoods."

Normalized, excessive speeding increases the risk of crash severity significantly, especially for people traveling around the city by walking, biking, or rolling. According to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety , a pedestrian struck at 20 mph has an 18% chance of sustaining a serious injury, but at 35 mph, the risk of serious injury climbs to 67%. Those risks are intensified thanks to the fondness for larger vehicle types in the U.S. compared to elsewhere in the world.

The issue of equitable camera placement has been front-and-center in the conversation around traffic camera expansion in Seattle over recent years. When SDOT was deciding how to double the school zone camera program in 2023, the department consciously selected school locations in more affluent areas in order to balance out camera locations that had been placed in neighborhoods with higher minority populations.

Several of the streets poised for 24/7 speed camera installation are also set to see physical upgrades that have the potential to reduce driver speeds through improved design. In Rainier Beach, SDOT is advancing plans to revamp Rainier Avenue between S Henderson Street and Ithaca Place S, as well as make changes to Seward Park Avenue S between Henderson and Rainier – including the interim installation of a new marked crossing and signal at Rainier Avenue S and 54th Avenue S by the end of the year.

On north Rainier Avenue, an even more substantive street rebuild remains in early stages, in an area where traffic safety advocates have been pushing for changes for years . That repaving project, being paired with a repave of S Henderson in Rainier Beach with a combined budget of more than $100 million dollars, is not set to be fully wrapped up until 2032.

Other cities around the region are also taking advantage of state's new camera authority, going even further than Seattle. Earlier this summer, Edmonds City Council voted to convert existing time-limited cameras at four different schools to 24/7 operation, citing the need to improve safety conditions around schools outside of the 90 minutes surrounding bell times on school days. Over a two-week period this summer, nearly 20,000 citations would have been issued to drivers traveling at least seven miles per hour over the normal speed limit, had the camera hours been expanded already.

Across Lake Washington in Bellevue, four new sets of 24/7 speed cameras near hospitals, parks, and school walk zones were installed in August, with another three locations eyed for implementation by the end of the year. Those new cameras garnered headlines when they were vandalized less than a week after installation , but that only represented a small setback for Bellevue's traffic camera program.

articles.title: What should Capitol Hill’s new ‘Low Pollution Neighborhood’ streets look like?
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Capitol Hill residents and business owners will have their first chance this month to shape the future of their streets and public spaces as Seattle kicks off community outreach for its $9.2 million Low-Pollution Neighborhoods pilot program.

The Seattle Department of Transportation will host an in-person public workshop on Sunday, September 27, from 1:00 PM to 4:00 PM at the Cathy Hillenbrand Community Room , located above Capitol Hill Station on 10th Ave E. The event is free and open to all, featuring food, project information, and opportunities to talk directly with city planners.

The meeting comes after Capitol Hill was selected alongside Lake City and South Park/Georgetown for the citywide pilot. Backed by $8 million in local transportation levy funds alongside federal support, the initiative is aimed at cutting car exhaust, cooling heat-island concrete, and making crossing the street safer.

“Pedestrianization and these types of streets are an ingredient to making a whole neighborhood that encourages use of transit, walking, cycling, and other modes,” SDOT climate officer Radcliffe Dacanay told CHS earlier this year. “It isn’t that a pedestrianized street reduces all emissions all at once. It’s part of a broader collective of efforts that are combined to make that impact on reduction.”

The city under the Wilson administration is ready to change how Seattle uses its streets and embracing new statewide “shared streets” laws that will allow the creation of more stretches of roadway that put pedestrians and bikes first.

On Capitol Hill, the challenge is fitting new street designs, uses, and experiments around dense housing, a robust nightlife economy, and transit. There will also be consideration of public safety and elements like lighting.

Priority areas under consideration include the Pike/Pine and Broadway cores. Barbara Bailey Way north of Cal Anderson adjacent the bustling light rail station is a popular choice for pedestrianization potential.

Community advocates hope the planning process will resurrect pedestrian-first concepts such as the long-sought Capitol Hill “Superblock” or the full pedestrianization of Barbara Bailey Way alongside the Sunday Farmers Market. Other ideas range from delivery curb-management hubs and EV freight loading zones to new mid-block crossings, green infrastructure, and expanded street-tree canopies.

There will also be hopes of avoiding past false starts. More than a decade ago, organizers closed a stretch of E Pike to vehicles for three Saturday nights in 2015 and repeated similar versions of the “pilot” until opposition from some nearby business and property owners shut the trials down.

City officials say that the new pilot remains in its listening phase. Feedback gathered on September 27 will help refine a design “toolbox” through 2027, with physical construction and programmatic rollouts slated to begin in 2028.
Registration for the workshop is optional, and community members can learn more and RSVP via SDOT’s Climate Response project portal .

articles.title: Following court win, Seattle Parks gathers input on Denny Blaine rules
articles.author: CHS
paras: The park had a busy summer of events including a visit from the Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence

By Brenna Gauchat More than 40 Seattleites gathered at the Miller Community Center on Tuesday evening to comment on Seattle Parks and Recreation’s proposed Denny Blaine Park Supplemental Use Guidelines , focusing on protecting its historically recognized LGBTQ+ clothing-optional beach.

The community meeting followed a favorable King County court ruling in July for the City of Seattle and Friends of Denny Blaine , a volunteer group dedicated to protecting the beach. The lawsuit was filed by Denny Blaine Park for All , a neighbor group seeking to prohibit nudity or close the park entirely.
The court ruling included mandatory directives that shape the updated guidelines, which will be implemented once the public comment period closes.

“We just want to be clear that several elements of what we’re proposing in this policy are set by court order and can’t be unilaterally changed by the City,” Justin Hellier , SPR’s Strategic Policy Advisor, said in response to community questions about which regulations in this non-negotiable list may become changeable in the future.

Court-ordered mandates require a map of designated clothing-optional and required areas, accessibility initiatives, and explicit definitions distinguishing legal from illegal behavior on park grounds.

“The City involved Friends of Denny Blaine and received our input on the park’s future. Nearly every proposal Friends of Denny made is reflected in these guidelines, including clarifications on critical language and listing nude recreation as an approved authorized use,” Simon Thornton , President of Friends of Denny Blaine, said about the group’s involvement in the process.
Thornton called the mandates a “major milestone” while offering concrete solutions during public comments to address remaining concerns.
Key issues outside the court order included non-consensual photography from neighboring private properties and measures to prevent sexual, verbal, or physical harassment.
The neighbor group Denny Blaine Park for All has posted images of beachgoers on its website.
SPR noted that regulating private property falls outside its jurisdiction. However, attendees suggested installing higher fences or strategic landscaping to block private views of the beach.
“Add one line to the park signage: ‘Please refrain from nonconsensual photography and video recording of parkgoers’,” Thornton suggested, noting it provides clear boundaries at minimal cost.
Both supporters and opponents agree safety from sexual misconduct — defined by SPR to include indecent exposure, assault, harassment, and lewd acts — is a priority.
Sexual misconduct has always been strictly prohibited at the park.
An attendee opposing relaxed rules shared a personal story of assault at the park, emphasizing the need for increased police or park ranger protection.
Thornton echoed this call, recommending “a single, posted point of contact at the kiosk or signage for parkgoers to report harassment.”

Thornton echoed this sentiment, suggesting, “a single, posted point of contact, at the kiosk or one the signage, for parkgoers to report harassment, so people know where to go when something happens.”
“I was thrilled to learn a place existed where queer folks and others can be in community in a space where nudity is not explicitly sexualized,” another attendee shared.
Hellier assured attendees that while current rules are constrained by the court order, SPR will periodically review the guidelines in the future.
The new guideline review runs parallel to broader community sessions starting late September regarding long-term park investments and improvements.

articles.title: Proposal would include Pike Place Market transportation oversight in Vision Zero overhaul of Seattle traffic laws
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: A package of legislation hoped to overhaul Seattle traffic safety will be up for committee debate Thursday at the Seattle City Council including a key proposed amendment that would strengthen the City Traffic Engineer’s jurisdiction while refining roadway oversight in the city.

Sponsored by Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck , a key amendment would strengthen the City Traffic Engineer’s authority across all city rights-of-way, explicitly including designated historic, landmark, and special review districts including Pike Place Market .
Changes in these areas currently face review by volunteer boards facilitated by the Department of Neighborhoods .

Two other individual proposals alter project administration and technical standards. One amendment grants the City Traffic Engineer sole discretion to determine whether capital projects materially alter street configuration or operation, requiring the transportation department to incorporate identified safety treatments when feasible. Another proposed amendment aligns traffic device definitions with federal standards and updates provisions regarding arterial speed limits, crash reporting, and intersection countermeasures.

CHS reported here on the council’s effort to write Vision Zero into Seattle law with speed limits, trash truck side guard rules, and faster action on deadly crashes under transportation committee head Rob Saka .

The complicated legislative push has come as Mayor Katie Wilson has accelerated SDOT construction projects already in the pipeline with her executive order streamlining Vision Zero pedestrian safety work. The executive order directs the Seattle Department of Transportation to fast-track high-priority safety improvements across high-crash corridors. Key measures include completing the SW Wildwood Place protected bike lane by late 2026, advancing Phase 2 of the 12th Ave S Safety Project, increasing intersection visibility through daylighting, and upgrading 19 high-collision locations along major routes like Aurora Ave N and Rainier Ave S.

For Saka’s process, Thursday’s committee session also includes uncontested changes grouped into a consent package modify additional operational details. One amendment expands the definition of vulnerable travelers to include individuals using wheelchairs, ambulatory aids, and other mobility devices. Another revision moves policy findings into non-binding recitals to prevent legal interpretations based on preliminary declarations. A separate amendment replaces specific mentions of a Vision Zero Plan with the broader term traffic safety program throughout code text. Other consent items set safety plan updates for roughly three-year intervals, soften review timelines involving the state transportation department, and replace strict mandates for 72-hour fatal crash site reviews and 14-day remediations with an evaluation of existing response procedures.
Further consent actions clarify shared safety duties across transportation divisions and expand vehicle side-guard safety recommendations for city contractors.

articles.title: Girls Own the Void and Art Owns Downtown
articles.author: Amanda Manitach
paras: The second half of September means Art + Culture Week is upon us. Recall how I previously mentioned September is Art World Prom in NYC? This week feels like a (much-needed) attempt to recalibrate the Seattle art calendar to match some of that energy. Now in its third year, the annual Art + Culture Week festival is designed to stack as many events as possible at as many galleries and venues as possible within the space of nine days. It’s a great way to get to know new spaces or get to know old ones better. Find the complete calendar of events here .

The keynote event is WALKDONTRUN , now in its second year, which turns downtown into an art-filled corridor. It’s gonna be gorgeous out, so unless you’re going to a wedding or a funeral, you better soak it up. Here are details about that plus some other things I recommend you catch in the coming weeks.

September 17 unpoetry at Frye Art Museum Our Genius shortlister Eric M. Acosta brings ekphrasis to life with the latest installation of unpoetry at the Frye . This one is inspired by the current exhibit I hear the hollow boom of time , with responsive works by dance artist Noelle Chun; composer, intermedia artist, poet, and archivist María Dolores A. Matienzo; and multi-instrumentalist Tom Scully, who is currently the guitarist for improvised noise duo CSTMR and “gunk-pop” band Black Ends. Project NW: David Hytone at Tacoma Art Museum For the past decade, David Hytone has been building a style and process that produces visual stunners—uncanny mixed-media quasi-landscapes on canvas that are populated with hypothetical dream architecture and objects not from the “real” world. His Project NW installation at Tacoma Art Museum leans even harder into nostalgia-tinged dream imagery and gently absurd symbolism (sinking toy ships and carnival roller coasters). He’s also utilized the space to introduce some massive pieces that tip traditional painting into the realm of installation.

September 17-19 The Goldberg Variations at On the Boards The word “unhinged” is the primary adjective used to describe Clayton Lee’s The Goldberg Variations , opening this week at On the Boards . What’s actually going to unfold onstage tonight is a surprise—each performance is different (you can read a review of the recent iteration at Portland’s Time-Based Art Festival here ), but I daresay we’ll be enraptured as Lee uses Bach and wrestling as a vehicle for teasing out fantasies delving into themes of “power dynamics, sexual desire, and vulnerability that entangles queer sexuality with classical music and professional wrestling.”

September 19 WALKDONTRUN The long-awaited WALKDONTRUN features more than 200 artists spread across 20 blocks of downtown Seattle. Find the full list here . This year, the route is reversed from last year’s, kicking off in Westlake Park at 11 a.m. and ending at Occidental Square. Here are my notes from print: Last year’s wayfinding was a little tricky. If that’s the case again, my advice is to study the route beforehand and plot a path so you don’t miss artists like Dez’Mon Omega Fair , one of my favorite performance artists in town; Charmi Shah , who is hiding collectable, baseball-card-size collages along the route for participants to find and keep; and Jesse Higman , whose interactive paint-pouring technique, performed around a massive tilting table , is an unforgettable experience. Or just wander blindly and let the art happen to you, because the magic of this event is that you get to experience the city in a completely new way.

Cut the Red Tape at Slip Gallery Seattle was shaped by redlining, a discriminatory housing practice that involved denying mortgages, insurance, or other financial services to Black, Asian American, and other communities of color in certain neighborhoods, resulting in wealth disparities and racial segregation. At Slip Gallery , Rodney King’s Cut the Red Tape addresses this city’s history of redlining and on Saturday the gallery hosts a panel discussion (noon–2 pm) featuring King and guest artists Myron Curry, TR Miles, Vincent Keele, and Jonarra Swanson to discuss gentrification, redlining, and how artists can shape what society remembers.

Social Contract at Actualize AiR Tommy Gregory and Rachael Comer have curated the fall exhibition at Actualize AiR , which features 17 artists from across the continental US, including The Stranger’ s very own Charles Mudede, whose video, Twilight of the Goodtimes , loops across a TV screen haunted by the fallout of late capitalism’s repeated calamities. I’m here for it. An opening reception is scheduled during WALKDONTRUN (4–8 pm) with an artist talk at 5.

September 20 Build Your Own Black Hole at Steve Gilbert Studio Do astrophysics the hedgewitch way with Meghan Thréinfhir ’s Build Your Own Black Hole workshop, from 3–6 pm at Steve Gilbert Studio . Thréinfhir will take you through her solo exhibition, Spacetime Gothic, which features her original black hole in a jar—an inky, liquidy ball of ferrofluid that dances with magnets and has the impeccable title Girls Own The Void (Land Art For Bog Witches) . All materials provided but the vessel—just bring a small jar, baby-food size recommended.

September 23 William Kentridge Anything Is Possible at Greg Kucera Gallery It’s movie night in the gallery. They’re screening the feature documentary William Kentridge Anything Is Possible along with short films by the artist (6–7:30 pm). The doc provides a BTS glimpse inside Kentridge’s studio practice and mind. The selection of shorts, featuring hand-drawn charcoal animations, explores his themes of memory, time, and all kinds of politics-ridden history.

September 24 Day-to-Day: A Life in Sticky Notes at Henry Art Gallery Artist Clare Johnson has kept a diaristic sticky note drawing practice for two decades, amassing a collection of over 6,000 drawings (and counting). Join Johnson for a talk and hands-on activities that will help you develop your own relationship to making “everyday” art. If you haven’t seen the Day-to-Day exhibition at Henry Art Gallery (I wrote about it here ), this is your sign.

Melissa Messer at Spectrum Fine Art Melissa Messer describes her practice and work as “if Rothko’s daughter were obsessed with form.” I might add Albers to the mix. Messer is a colorist whose use of hue is almost spiritual (in which case, Rothko is the correct comparison). She is also a pre-eminent figurative painter, where the human body becomes an armature upon which to drape shades of deciduous greens, burnt orange, and acid gold. This is Messer’s first solo with Spectrum Fine Art ; a formal reception lands on October 8, but you can get a preview this weekend for Art + Culture Week.

September 26 Kelly Bjork: Lunacy at J. Rinehart Gallery No one in this city is as cool and talented as Kelly Bjork . Her drawings are full of intimacies and bodies, tenderness and acceptance, rendered in beautiful, illustrative precision. Her second solo exhibition at J. Rinehart Gallery , Lunacy , addresses queerness in a time of queer discrimination and violence. The exhibition preview opens today, 1–3 pm.

This year’s artists include Anouk Rawkson, Jordan Christianson, Shiloh Davies, Shari Noble, Brandon Vosika, Jersey Virago, Dez’Mon Fair, Mariel Andrade, Devon Yan, Ruben David Rodriguez, and Debora Spencer.

articles.title: Charlie’s Queer Books Is Opening a Second Location
articles.author: Katie Lee Ellison
paras: This is the best books news I’ve heard since Roxane Gay and Debbie Millman bought The Rumpus : Charlie’s Queer Books is opening a new location in Seattle’s original gayborhood, Capitol Hill. Next door to Unicorn Bar, across the street from Wildrose, and around the corner from Elliott Bay Book Company, this new space is set to open in November.

The new store will be ADA accessible and twice as big as the Fremont location, with an events and gathering space with room for 50 seats, as well as a coffee shop and wine bar. I spoke with the owners, Charlie Hunts and Madeline Burchard, about how it all came to be.

How did you get to a place where you could open a second location? Hunts: It has been remarkable how the Seattle queer and literary community have rallied around us. At this point, we’ve run out of space. Not only on the shelves, but also in terms of what this [current] location can handle for events and as a gathering space.

The property managers of this new location are an older couple from 12th & Pike St. Associates. They understand not only what we’re doing, but why it’s important for the neighborhood. If you keep the rent at a manageable price, even if it’s still high, you can keep the businesses that make the neighborhood what it is and encourage the vitality of that space.

How important are exclusively queer bookstores these days? Burchard: Because we’re in a cross section of record book bans and anti-LGBT legislation, our bookstore holds more responsibility than the average small business. That is in the forefront of our minds every single day we open the door. It’s been touching, the way people look to us to be leaders in the community, especially when something happens that affects the community.

Do you feel ready and able for that responsibility? Burchard: Charlie and I have training for it, but it’s heavy to be like, “Okay, we gotta say the responsible thing. I hope we’re getting this right.” We won’t always, but I hope we can show up for people in the best way. Sometimes it’s tough for me to figure out our next step—what we say, what we do, or if people even want to hear from us about it. But we have a lot of young trans customers who look up to Charlie in particular. So Charlie’s is more than a third space. This is part of our social fabric.

Hunts: We also do things like watch parties and video nights. Events that are kind of stupid, silly, but essential. That’s one of our niches—to not take ourselves too seriously, to be joyful, and in touch with culture, too. We’re not just people who own a bookstore selling to gay people. We are gay people.

Do you have a vision or hopes and dreams for where this is all headed, say five years from now? Hunts: We’ve had big hand-wavy dreams, like what if this became a national thing? But it’s very hypothetical. Right now, we’re entering a new industry in coffee and food service. We’re getting a handle on that, and what’s great about this place is it allows us to support programming that doesn’t charge for tickets. So everything from a silent book club to open mic, it helps support community events and bigger authors, too.

I think our vision for the store is people come in here and they’re kind of entering into an alternate universe where they are the norm. They are the defaults. They’re not hunting the shelves for things that wreck them. They’re not in the LGBT section that’s tucked away.

Like the porn section or something. Hunts: Yes, we are always next to self-help. We have encountered bookstores where the LGBT section is next to porn, self-help. Sometimes in… a literal closet. A little closet that just didn’t have a door on it. We were like, we have to make this bookstore.

Is there anything you want to say to people about the new space? Hunts: I’m excited to keep iterating on this business, see how far we can take it, and learn as much as we can. We’re very open. Folks who came in and said, “I want to start a book club”: we let them start a book club. If folks have dreams for something, they don’t always have a space for it. We are open to these conversations. If someone is serious, they want to take charge of it, work with us, and collaborate, let’s talk about it.

articles.title: Slog AM: Robert Kraft Says He’ll Donate $2 Million to “Humanitarian Aid” After Macklemore Pledges $1 million to Palestine, Downtown Seattle Is Booming, Federal Reserve Increases the Cost of Borrowing
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: The average price a worker pays to commute in the Seattle area? $10,018 a year, according to a study by Consumer Affairs . And the amount of time a worker spends driving to and from a job? An hour, which is “roughly 10 full days spent [in a car annually].” Altogether, only four metropolitan areas are above ours when it comes to bleeding through the nose to get around. Automobile freedom not only doesn’t exist, it’s not cheap.

But how is the new bus lane on Denny Way going? Over the past two weeks, I’ve taken the 8 bus 10 times during rush hour, and not a single bus was late. None. Not only that, traffic jams appear to have vanished from this part of Denny Way. Where did they go? What kind of sorcery is this? Losing a lane has actually loosened rush-hour traffic? Maybe I’m just seeing things. Time will tell.

It rained on Sunday. And it was almost like real rain, the kind of rain that falls for days and makes this region dark and green like the forests in the Twilight movies. But the rain on Sunday departed around noon and, so far, refuses to return. What a tease. Today will be mostly clear and sunny. Expect a high of 75.

U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez does it again. She voted with Republicans on a measure that advanced their priorities. She was one of two defections on this matter. If both “Democrats” had voted against the measure, it would have failed . The problem is this: The GOP is no longer a party. It’s just Trump. So, if you support a Republican measure, you are only supporting Trump and his massive anti-democratic project. Perez is not a centrist, as the Seattle Times keeps calling her. There is nothing like a center in US politics today.You are with Trump or you are not. It’s that simple, Perez.

Downtown Seattle is once again far from dying . It is in fact thriving. Last month, this part of town, with its waterfront, its markets, hotels, galleries, stadiums, and Link stations experienced 9.2 million visits . This is, according to data collected by an organization that has it in for Mayor Katie Willson , the Downtown Seattle Association , the busiest the downtown has been since July 2019. The DSA also reported that consumers spent an estimated $165 million in July.

Well, Trump did not get his wish —cheap cash—from the very man he placed at the top of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh. Yesterday, he raised interest rates “for the first time in more than three years” because inflation is a real thing; something, anything has to be done to cool it. Rates went up by 25 basis points and are now in the 3.75 percent–4 percent range. The inflation Warsh is now battling by raising the cost of borrowing was entirely caused by Trump’s war and tariffs.

Black holes not only consume everything in sight but also expel large amounts of gas. Astronomers at the University of Florence verified this phenomenon while observing a black hole at the center of a galaxy, NGC 1066 (also called the Squid Galaxy), which is 45 million light-years from us. This black hole is a monster. It’s between “8 million and 17 million solar masses,” and it ejects much more gas than scientists expected. (This extra gas is hard to detect because it is dust poor.) But get this: The astronomers also “checked whether this gas could ever fall back toward the black hole. Comparing the outflow’s speed with the galaxy’s escape velocity, they found the gas is moving several times faster than needed to escape entirely.” The mystery of black holes only knows how to grow.

Let’s picture this. Some physicists believe, understandably, that the universe is actually the interior of a black hole. But how to make sense of this hypothesis? For one, it means the beginning is a singularity, the collapse of a dead star, and we are not moving toward it but bouncing from it. This means that in fact we are moving back in time. What we feel to be the past is actually in the future; and the past, where the singularity is located, is actually moving forward in time. This explains the nature of memory and computation. It is the future from which we are receding. And the actual past is the event horizon, which, as we approach, appears to be expanding at an accelerating rate. We call this acceleration toward the black hole’s past dark energy.

Macklemore keeps winning his war with Robert Kraft , the billionaire who forced Ed Sheeran, a coward whose music is to my ears what a wet stone is to my mouth, to drop the Seattle rapper from his Loop Tour. Macklemore challenged Kraft to match his $1 million pledge directly to Palestinian organizations, and, according to NYT , Kraft pledged $2 million to “the region.” Make of that what you will.

Linton Kwesi Johnson (also known as LKJ) is a dub poet. Dub is an abstract form of reggae, and in the late ’70s, Jamaican poets like Prince Far I and Mutabaruka used the echoing and reverberating dub rhythms as backdrops to their politically charged poems. LKJ was born in Jamaica, raised in the United Kingdom, educated as a sociologist, and was once a member of the British chapter of the Black Panther party. He used the dub-poem form to address the social and political realities of Britain’s depressed inner cities, particularly during the Thatcher years.

LKJ read (and still reads) his poetry with a thick and sometimes impenetrable Jamaican accent. For example, on “Reggae Fi Dada” (Making History, 1984), he opens with these lines: “Galang dada, galang gwwaan yaw sah/yu nevvah ad noh life fi live/jus di wan life fi give/yu did yu time pan ert/yu nevvah get yu jus dizert” (translation: “Go on daddy, go on, go on sir/you never had no life to live/just the one life to give/you did your time upon the earth/you never got your just dessert”). Some of LKJ’s dub poems surrender all meaning to the hypnotic pulse of the reggae rhythm, such as the title track of the 1978 album Dread Beat an’ Blood , which moves to a slow and bouncy reggae beat.

Today is your last chance to see the documentary about LKJ, Dread Beat an’ Blood , at the theater that won this year’s Genius Award for film, the Beacon Cinema . Because I can’t say enough about LKJ, let’s conclude AM with his masterpiece, and atheist anthem (yes, this enlightened dread does not believe in Jah), “ Reality Poem .”

articles.title: Free Will Astrology
articles.author: Rob Brezsny
paras: ARIES (March 21-April 19): Realities you’ve been oblivious to will soon pop into view. Hints and signals you’ve been unconsciously pushing away will start flocking toward you. A lingering emotional numbness will thaw, and surges of feelings will pour into your awareness. Warning! At first, it may feel like an overload: too much sopping wet data arriving too quickly for you to organize or interpret. If you’re willing to be patient and focus on slowly metabolizing the influx, though, the apparent chaos will ultimately weave itself into a luminous web of new understanding.

TAURUS (April 20-May 20): In Peru’s Andean mountains, Indigenous and smallholder farmers cultivate a rich diversity of potato varieties, continuing a farming tradition rooted in the crop’s domestication thousands of years ago. Each variety thrives in slightly different soil, altitude, and climate. By planting many types at once, the farmers ensure that at least some crops will flourish no matter what conditions arise. I suggest you apply this way of thinking to your own life in the coming weeks, Taurus. Diversify your efforts instead of depending on a single plan or expectation. Plan for multiple small initiatives that will evolve with unique growth patterns.

GEMINI (May 21-June 20): In biology, many organisms survive harsh or unpredictable conditions by entering dormancy. This is a reversible state of greatly reduced metabolism and development. Seeds, spores, and the dormant stages of some small animals can remain viable for years until cues such as water, temperature, light, or nutrients signal that conditions are favorable again. Then they can resume growth, development, or activity, often rapidly. I suspect you may experience a comparable upsurge in the coming weeks, Gemini. A project or aspiration that seemed inert may reawaken and reignite.

CANCER (June 21-July 22): Novelist Kurt Vonnegut advised us to try some task that scares us every day of our lives. That may be a viable experiment for a Scorpio like him, but is it a wise prescription for us Cancerians, who like to feel secure and protected? Normally, I would say no. I’d recommend that you and I dare ourselves to wrestle with one of our fears no more than once per month. But the coming weeks may warrant a departure from our typical rhythms. I suspect we can fortify our long-term safety and peace through more frequent encounters with unpredictable episodes that rouse our hidden reserves of courage.

LEO (July 23-Aug. 22): The ancient Greeks believed that the goddess Harmonia presided over the blending of opposites into balanced beauty. Her dad was the god of war and her mom the goddess of love, so she had a lot of practice. In her line of work, tension between different forces could produce elegant unity rather than conflict. In alignment with astrological omens, I’ve appointed Harmonia to be your guardian angel in the coming weeks, Leo. I urge you to call on her dynamically and frequently. Rifts and splits and divisions that have never before been possible to heal are now swayable by the collaborative efforts of you and the goddess.

VIRGO (Aug. 23-Sept. 22): If I were writing this horoscope for the Gun Lovers’ Gambling Porn website, I might counsel my Virgo readers to maintain strict control over their wickedness, debauchery, and decadence. Why? Because now is a time when vices and sins are even more likely than usual to sow chaos and spawn big messes. However, since you are reading my oracle in a more genteel publication and are almost certainly a refined person of high integrity, I’m confident there will be minimal uproar if I dare you to tap into your raw animal energy and unruly instinctual nature. I believe it’s time to at least experiment with wilder aspects of your deep self.

LIBRA (Sept. 23-Oct. 22): The Real You and the Semi-Real You have been embroiled in a showdown with the False You. This is as tough and heroic a struggle as you’ve had to deal with in quite some time, though it has often been subtle and partially cloaked. I am of course rooting for the Real You and the Semi-Real You to emerge victorious from the conflict, though I also hope you don’t feel the need to humiliate and crush the False You. That part of you has sometimes served a valuable purpose and doesn’t deserve to be trashed. And what will become of the Semi-Real You after this drama is finished? I suggest you give it a modest place in your repertoire. Like the False You, it sometimes proves to be useful.

SCORPIO (Oct. 23-Nov. 21): Hummingbirds can fly backward. They’re the only birds capable of sustained reverse flight. This requires extraordinary wing flexibility and energy expenditure, but it gives them access to nectar that forward-only fliers have more difficulty sampling. Let’s treat this as a useful metaphor for you in the coming weeks, Scorpio. It may be that your progress and success won’t always come from advancing. Some rich resources may require the equivalent of reverse flight. Consider returning to conversations you thought were finished, revisiting places you’d mentally filed away as “done,” and extracting value from sources you’ve already passed by.

SAGITTARIUS (Nov. 22-Dec. 21): In chemistry, catalysts are substances that accelerate reactions without being consumed in the process. A tiny amount of catalyst can dramatically transform how quickly elements combine. An example is the enzyme catalase in our cells, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide (a byproduct of our metabolism) into water and oxygen millions of times faster than it would decompose on its own. I believe you are now in a phase when your catalytic powers are at a peak, Sagittarius. Be careful where you point that potency of yours! Make sure you really want to change what you’re capable of changing.

CAPRICORN (Dec. 22-Jan. 19): Every species adapts to its surroundings. Even harmful microbes evolve over time in order to survive. Syphilis, for instance, was once ferociously swift and deadly, but that intensity limited how far it could spread. So a gentler strain gradually evolved that allowed its hosts to live longer and pass it on more widely. Let this serve as a metaphor for how you handle your dark moods, odd compulsions, and brief bouts of craziness. Befriend the mild, manageable versions of these states and give them space to be felt and understood. Over time, the harsher, more destructive versions will lose ground and fade from power.

AQUARIUS (Jan. 20-Feb. 18): Paleontologists know that some dinosaurs traveled in herds with a specific formation: the most vulnerable members gathered in the center, protected by stronger individuals on the perimeter. It was a savvy way to run things, ensuring the group would thrive. I hope you’re willing to borrow some dinosaur wisdom, Aquarius. The coming weeks will be a good time to apply it to your own life. Who or what needs protection? What vulnerable projects or relationships deserve to be surrounded and shielded? Are you willing and able to use your strength to guard what’s tender and growing? Be a shepherd, a steward, a defender.

PISCES (Feb. 19-March 20): In ancient times, Hawaii’s Coconut Island was renowned for its healing powers—but on one condition. Those who sought its medicinal help couldn’t just expect the local spirits to do all the work, but had to take part in awakening the magic. Legend tells us that a seeker could be cured by swimming three times around the island. This participatory approach to healing mirrors your current situation, Pisces. You are close to a source of renewal, but if you hope to unlock its full strength, you must coax it out with your ingenuity.
Homework: What’s the most important question for you to answer in the next year?

articles.title: Oregon Lawmakers Seek to Open Up Affordable Housing Records Following ProPublica’s Reporting
articles.author: Rob Davis
paras: Two Oregon lawmakers want to end an unusual exemption in the state’s records law that has kept the public from learning how hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayer money is spent on subsidized housing — and the effort has already landed key industry support.

Rep. Pam Marsh, chair of Oregon’s House Committee on Housing and Homelessness, told ProPublica that she plans to introduce legislation next year to eliminate a law that shields key details of state spending on low-income housing .

The southern Oregon Democrat said she didn’t realize the documents were being kept secret until reading about it in a ProPublica story. She said previous leaders of her committee told her they were also unaware.
“I think this is an issue that will have very broad interest,” Marsh said.
State Sen. Khanh Pham, a Portland Democrat and chair of the Senate Committee on Housing and Development, said she also wants the Legislature to tackle the issue in its next session.

Meanwhile, a lobbying group for low-income housing developers, lenders and related businesses, Housing Oregon, said it strongly supports repealing the secrecy provision; the organization has asked the state to disclose more about projects that it funds in the meantime.

“Oregon’s affordable housing providers share the public’s interest in ensuring that public investments in housing are used effectively, responsibly, and with visibility,” said Kevin Cronin, a spokesperson for the group. “The questions raised in your recent ProPublica article regarding development costs deserve serious attention.”
Cronin said Oregon can increase transparency around development costs “while still protecting genuinely proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”
“More consistent reporting of costs and outcomes will help policymakers, providers, researchers, and the public understand where the system is working and where it needs improvement,” Cronin said.

ProPublica highlighted Oregon’s secrecy around low-income housing in August. Since 2021, our story noted, Oregon has given developers an unprecedented $1.4 billion, and the cost of developing each low-income apartment has nearly doubled, to $540,000. Dozens of projects are lined up for another $850 million in future state funding, and costs are expected to continue rising.

“We are spending, as you said, a lot of money on the development of affordable housing,” Marsh said. “We really need to understand what it is that we’re funding, how much it costs, why it costs that much, and be able to justify the investments that we’re making.”
In other states, researchers and journalists have used the financial records from subsidized housing projects to investigate their spiraling costs and the drivers behind the growing price tag.

Marsh said after reading the ProPublica story that she “pretty much immediately” looked up the provision in Oregon public records law that officials cite for keeping cost details secret. She said financial documents that show where a project’s money is coming from and what it’s going to should be public and easily accessed. She said she would like to see them posted online as part of the public materials that Oregon’s Housing Stability Council receives for each project before awarding subsidies.

Pham, in a written statement, said: “It’s imperative that Oregonians can trust that our state government is investing in affordable housing as cost-effectively as possible. I appreciated ProPublica’s reporting on Oregon’s inadequate public records law that hinders our ability to monitor how affordable housing funds are being spent, and I’m hopeful legislators can address this next year.”

Oregon’s Sunshine Committee, which reviews public records exemptions and recommends ones that could be rolled back, is also examining the exemption for housing financials as a result of ProPublica’s coverage, co-chair Charlie Fisher said.

It’s not clear where opposition to repeal efforts, if any, might arise. Officials in Washington and California, where the details of state spending on subsidized housing are available to the public, have said it hasn’t interfered with low-income housing efforts.

Oregon Housing and Community Services, the state housing agency that persuaded lawmakers to create the records exemption in 1997, cited the law in redacting major sections of developers’ cost reports that ProPublica requested in May.
The agency’s current executive director, Andrea Bell, told ProPublica in July that she is committed to transparency but that the agency is following the law as it stands today.

Asked to comment this week about whether the agency would support efforts to change the law, a spokesperson said by email that state agencies don’t take positions on bills. “OHCS appreciates the opportunity to review the legislation” that’s introduced in 2027, the spokesperson wrote.

articles.title: Robert Kraft, once the NFL’s good guy, is just another billionaire silencing Macklemore | Howard Bryant
articles.author: Howard Bryant
paras: The Patriots owner’s decision to ban the rapper from performing at the team’s stadium brings back memories of the blackballing of Colin Kaepernick

Six years ago, in the middle of a “racial reckoning” that never was, a White House that had begun out of control reached its chaotic apex. Federal officials were sweeping citizens off American streets in unmarked vehicles , surrounding the Lincoln Memorial with armed guards and rolling military vehicles through residential neighborhoods in a fascist reaction to protests against the murder of George Floyd. It was at this point that NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, realizing it had all gone too far, appeared on a Zoom and admitted his league was “wrong” for not listening to its players when they had protested against police brutality.

The implication was clear: more than any other sports league, the NFL was harshest in its reaction to the protests that began with Trayvon Martin in 2012 and continued with Ferguson, Baltimore and Colin Kaepernick. By blackballing Kaepernick, sitting by while broadcast partners refused to air the national anthem to undermine the protests, and, most embarrassingly, Goodell’s draconian announcement that teams would be subject to fines if players showed dissent, the NFL had proven itself to act in the most un-American of ways.

You’ve been performing since the late 80s. What keeps you going? AmongstTheWaves It’s a good question. I don’t really know any other life. articles.title: I’m nearly 30, a virgin and feel lonely. The manosphere is trying to draw me in – where else can I seek assurance? | Leading questions
articles.author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
paras: The manosphere says this type of suffering is targeted neglect, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith . But your suffering gives you the ability to make your part of the world better.
I’m approaching 30 and I’m still a kissless virgin.

I’ve suffered with depression and anxiety since childhood and my family isn’t the most functional or supportive. I don’t really have friends either, as I find it hard to connect with others due to being bullied and feeling that I’m not worthwhile or wanted. I was also homeschooled from 14 and moved to a different part of the country at 15 and a few more times since then, so I feel quite rootless and alienated.

articles.title: Trump’s love of fossil fuels is about more than money | Moira Donegan
articles.author: Moira Donegan
paras: The US decision to remove limits on coal and gas plant emissions is rooted in a perception of manliness in these industries

You can impress a certain kind of person at a party by reciting the fact that there are more yoga instructors in the US than there are coalminers. In fact, the disparity is greater than this catchy phrasing suggests: there are actually more yoga instructors in the US than there are people employed in the entirety of the coalmining industry, miners and otherwise. It’s not even especially close: about 38,000 people in the US work in coal, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics , compared to about 100,000 yoga instructors who are registered with the Yoga Alliance, an industry group.

If you looked only at the numbers, you might think a politician would be incentivized to talk about the interests of the yoga industry, about the dignity that yoga jobs give to American families, or about the need to foster growth in the yoga industry, more than they talk about these things for coal; after all, yoga, not coal, is putting food on the table in more American households. But no politician would ever talk about the interests of yoga teachers, or wax poetic about their role in the American dream, the way they do with coal miners; if they did, they’d be laughed out of the room. And we all know why: yoga is thought of as decadent, cosmopolitan and feminine, while coal mining is imagined as hardscrabble, honorable and masculine.

articles.title: Iran war pushes diesel – the economy’s lifeblood – to record high prices, with no relief on the horizon
articles.author:
<name>Morgan Bazilian, Professor of Public Policy and Director of the Payne Institute, Colorado School of Mines</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/morgan-bazilian-798291"/>
paras: Diesel fuel prices in the U.S. continue to break all-time records, hitting $6.28 a gallon as a national average on Sept. 14, 2026, and they aren’t likely to come down anytime soon. Because diesel is the fuel for freight transportation, farming and construction – and is related to a key heating fuel – the effects are set to spread across the entire U.S. economy.

The inflation-adjusted price of diesel in late August was about as high as it was in 2022 and has likely risen further. There are still three factors that we, scholars of U.S. and global energy markets and supply chains , see that set the stage for prices to remain high and potentially climb even further.

Two of these elements – environmental protection regulations on oil refineries and Russia’s war with Ukraine – have been building tension for years. But the situation has been pushed into a crisis by the U.S. war against Iran , which has closed the Strait of Hormuz to a large percentage of oil and refined products shipments for more than six months.
Amid that crisis, U.S. oil refineries are making lots of money .

In mid-September 2026, diesel prices were up 67% over September 2025’s monthly national average of $3.75 a gallon , and they have risen sharply since. In January 2026, before the U.S. and Israel first attacked Iran in late February, the average diesel price in the U.S. was lower, at $3.52 a gallon – meaning that diesel prices have jumped more than 78% since the war began.
In part, that’s because the country, and the world, have been losing diesel refining capacity for many years and can’t just ramp up production to fill the shortages.

Starting in 2006, U.S. federal regulations were phased in that required refiners to produce diesel fuel with far less sulfur than had previously been allowed. The regulations were intended to reduce air pollution and acid rain precursors mainly from trucks and buses . The resulting fuel was much cleaner . In 2014, the rules were applied to locomotives and marine vehicles.

U.S. refineries had to install expensive equipment to comply, which took years and billions of dollars . This, in turn, increased costs between 5 and 9 cents per gallon . And the fuel contains slightly less energy per unit of volume – so a larger quantity of low-sulfur diesel is required to meet the demand.

Only one refinery, in Galveston, Texas , has been built in the past 50 years , and at 45,000 barrels per day it meets less than 0.2% of U.S. demand. In 2025, two refineries shut down due to poor economic performance. And since 2020, more than a dozen others have converted to producing renewable diesel to take advantage of federal and state biofuel incentives, but that conversion can cut the amount of actual fuel they produce at least in half, according to our estimates.

As a result, the remaining refineries are running flat out. Crude going into refineries reached about 17.5 million barrels a day in late August, and refineries were operating at nearly 98% of their maximum capacity – the highest level since 2018. Even so, output of distillate , which includes diesel and related fuels such as heating oil and jet fuel, was lower than in 2025.
Distillate inventories held by refiners, distributors and retailers fell to about 103 million barrels by late August, the lowest for that point in the calendar since 1951.
As U.S. inventories of diesel fell in August, the country’s diesel exports hit a record high as the global market sought to fill supplies normally provided by Russia.

Historically the world’s second-largest diesel exporter after the United States, Russia banned exports of diesel on July 9, 2026 , to ensure supplies for its military. In September, the country extended the export ban until the end of 2026 in the wake of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries.
Middle Eastern refiners, also key to global diesel supplies, have scaled back production because of disruptions from the war with Iran .
Together, these forces mean the supply for diesel is very tight .
On Sept. 15, 2026, U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune proposed the U.S. ban diesel exports to increase domestic availability.

Even before the crisis in the Persian Gulf, the U.S. Energy Information Administration reported several factors were pushing diesel prices upward, including large exports to Europe , a cold winter in the Northeast in 2025-26 and high freight demand .
With the war continuing, refinery companies are taking advantage of the low supply – and their inability to make a whole lot more diesel – to charge more than ever for diesel fuel.

By late August, short-term profit margins for making diesel – called “ crack spreads ” in the industry – surpassed $100 per barrel for the first time ever, clearly showing demand for the fuel is well outpacing supply, as well as demand for crude oil itself.
What this means is that truckers, drivers and shipping companies are paying more for diesel – costs that are passed on to consumers. At the same time, refinery companies are seeing large profits .
The vast majority of the diesel fuel used in the U.S. is for transportation, mostly trucking . Other significant users are the railroad, agriculture, construction and marine industries.

A congressional Joint Economic Committee analysis in September 2026 found that higher diesel prices added more than $1.4 billion to the cost of planting major U.S. crops in 2026 versus 2025, a 63% increase, with Illinois, Iowa and Minnesota hit hardest. Because nearly every retail item travels by truck at some point, the diesel spike also feeds slowly into broader consumer inflation.

And there’s one more hit coming: Heating oil, which is chemically closely related to diesel, is a key heating fuel in the northeastern U.S. The latest projection from the Energy Information Administration expects national distillate inventories to fall below 100 million barrels in September and stay at that level through much of 2027. That’s lower than it has been since 2021, and heating oil prices for the coming winter are already up 30% or more .

The Middle East conflict is having wide-reaching implications. While crude oil prices are now above $100 per barrel, it is diesel, the fuel that much of the economy runs on, that is feeling the greatest stress.
And as refiners run flat out, any interruption would reduce production, as happened after a power outage at a Mobil refinery in Illinois on Sept. 13.
With falling stockpiles, even a sudden end to the Iran war is unlikely to yield significantly lower prices anytime soon.
In addition to being a fellow at the Payne Center, Jamie Webster also works in the Energy practice at Boston Consulting Group, which assists companies around the world across all energy types.
