articles.title: She’s Sporty Every Day
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: Everyone has a pop culture moment that runs on a loop in their idle mind, right? For me it’s the James Bond–style title sequence to Spice World . In the film, each Spice Girl is introduced with a candy-colored silhouette while singing the sparkly slow jam “Too Much.” The camera pans to a young Melanie C, aka Sporty Spice, who belts, “What part of no don’t you understand? I want a man, not a boy who thinks he caaaan.” I get chills when I think about it. Like their signature garb, each Spice Girl had a signature sound they brought to the group. For Melanie C, it was her powerful vocal timbre that usually came in with punchy, mic-drop-worthy lyrics.

The Spice Girls have lived on through multiple reunions, as well as in our hearts, our ponytails, our platform sneakers, and our bad British accents. But back in 1999, Melanie C was ready to shed her Sporty Spice identity. She chopped her signature brunette ponytail off and bleached her hair. She replaced her loose tracksuits with fitted baby tees and leather jackets. She released her debut solo album, Northern Star , which leaned into a moodier rock, trip-hop, and trance sound. Now, on her ninth album, Sweat , Melanie C is finally ready to return to her Sporty roots. Ahead of her solo show at the Showbox this weekend, I had the pleasure of chatting with Melanie C about all things Sweat, girl power, and her iconic gold tooth. She also confirmed that she will be performing a few Spice Girls songs at the show. “For fans who have never seen the Spice Girls live,” she told me, “this is your chance to see at least one of them!”

Your new album, Sweat, feels almost like a return to Sporty Spice. Were you thinking about your Sporty Spice identity while creating this album? One hundred percent. On the album, I’ve not only gone back to Sporty, but I’ve gone back before Sporty. My passion for dance music began in my late teens, and the Spice Girls came along soon after. I didn’t have a lot of opportunities to go out clubbing and socializing. It’s something that got left behind until I started DJing again about eight years ago, and with that, reuniting the Spice Girls in 2019. During that time, I not only rediscovered house and dance music, but also Sporty Spice. I realized that Sporty wasn’t a persona I took on; it was something that lived within me. It was so beautiful to have that realization. Once I found her again, I was like, I’m never letting her go. Sweat was the perfect outlet for bringing who I am as a DJ closer to who I am as a solo artist. Merging those worlds has just been such a fantastic experience.

Can you share some of your musical inspirations for the album? Madonna is my ultimate inspiration. I love that she’s released such an incredible dance record at the same time as me. Also, Robyn: I was so lucky to record the album in Stockholm and have dinner with her. At the time, she was also making [ Sexistential ] with her longtime collaborator Klas Åhlund, so I got some insight into how those two work. It was a really beautiful experience to have while working on the album. I was also inspired by young musicians like Charli XCX and Rose Gray—they grew up listening to the Spice Girls, and now I’m such a huge fan of theirs.

What should fans expect on your current tour? I think the overall feel is that it’s a live show, but with a club element. It’s not just going to a gig, but you’ll feel like you’ve had a night out, which is exactly what I wanted to create. Touring in North America, I am stopping in cities I’ve never played in as a solo artist. It’s been so beautiful to see the fans that I’ve grown up with—now in their 30s—who’ve been Spice Girls fans since they were kids. I’m also seeing new generations of young people with their mums. It’s a beautiful atmosphere. It feels really joyous, and there’s so much love. And even though I’m showcasing new work from Sweat , I pay respect to my Spice Girls roots. We do a few Spice Girls songs every night. There’s a newness, but there’s also nostalgia. With the help of the audience, I’ve been able to achieve exactly what I wanted to.

You’ve written so many songs, both as a solo artist and in the Spice Girls. What lyric are you most proud of? The lyric I always think about is “Live your life without regret / Don’t be someone who they forget,” from “Northern Star.” I’ve seen people have this tattooed on them. I think if we all had our time again, we’d do things differently. But I think it’s really important to acknowledge where you are, and you wouldn’t be in that place if it weren’t for all of the choices that you’ve made. That is a lyric that really resonates with me.

I saw an interview recently with Mel B, who said that she sometimes plays dress-up in her old Scary Spice outfits. Do you ever throw on your old tracksuits or pull out your Sporty Spice doll to indulge in that type of nostalgia? I’ve just realized how ridiculous I am as a human being. [ Laughs ] Okay, so I wear the same clothes that I’ve always worn. I’m sporty every day. I mean, I have a really fun wardrobe on stage, but my Adidas tracksuits are with me at all times. And actually, my Sporty Spice doll is on the road with me. She almost needs her own Instagram account… she is living it up! So yeah, I am quite ridiculous. I haven’t really changed.

Maybe this is a weird question, but I am dying to know more about your gold tooth that you used to have. Why did you get it and why did you get it removed? I actually have a tooth gem [ opens mouth and points to tooth ]. The placement is very inspired by you. Oh, I just love tooth gems! I’m very tempted to get one, but my daughter said that I’m too old. I might just turn up at home with one. [ Laughs ] It would be all sparkly onstage. I want to look into that. It’s so funny, isn’t it? [The gold tooth] was a little bit like my tattoos. When I was lucky enough to become a pop star with the Spice Girls, I just felt like there were no rules. You know, we could do whatever we wanted. I’d always wanted a gold tooth, so I just did it. It was just a veneer on the front of my tooth. As I got older, I thought maybe I’d grow up and be a little bit more sensible, so I had it removed. But I’m a bit like, oh, I wish I still had it! It was just a fun choice. I also had my nose pierced. It’s just one of those things you experience as a young person—you want to explore and change your appearance.

Did you feel like you were in control of curating your image in the Spice Girls? Yeah, I think it was interesting because I love OG Sporty. That’s really what I look back on and what inspires me with the outfits that I wear now. But I think as a young person, I got bored quickly. I tried to evolve her, but the original Sporty was the best.

Did you ever find yourself wanting to reject Sporty Spice? Do you know? I don’t think I ever wanted to reject her, but I think I was really keen for people to see that there was more to me than Sporty Spice, especially during my first solo album. We live in a world where we feel comfortable putting things and people in boxes, and I was frustrated because I knew there was more to me. So at that point, I suppose I was trying to look different: I physically cut all my hair off and had a little rebellious moment. But yeah, I’m very happy to come home to Sporty. I feel quite literally more comfortable.

I have to ask about Spice World because that movie was huge for me. What is your favorite memory from filming Spice World ? That was a crazy time, because it was like right in the middle of what I call Spicemania—those days from like ’96 to ’98. We were on set in London. We shot it in six weeks at all of these iconic locations. But not only that, we were shooting the movie while we were writing the second album, Spiceworld . We’d often have a mobile studio on set. We’d finish a day of shooting, then start recording. It was such a hectic time, but it was also so fun because everything we did was huge at that point. We were really achieving all of these crazy dreams that we’d set out to do. We were just lapping it up at that time.

One thing that mesmerized me as a kid was the Spice Bus in the movie. Was the Spice Bus anything like the real Spice Girls tour bus? Well, this is going to be a heartbreaker, but we flew everywhere! [ Laughs sadly ] We did have a tour bus briefly in 1998, but we didn’t go on it very often. It wasn’t until later in my solo career that I truly embraced the idea of a tour bus.

The film Spice World is a mockumentary, but was there any part of the film that was true to life? The movie was very much inspired by—but of course a huge exaggeration of—things that were actually happening. I mean, some of it wasn’t that exaggerated, but a lot of it was inspired by experiences that we’d had, so it did feel so close to the truth. We didn’t really have to act too much. I think there’s quite a lot of eye-rolling for me when Geri [Ginger Spice] speaks, isn’t there? That’s very true to life. [ Laughs ]

That brings me to my last question: what’s the meaning of “girl power”? I think it’s that thing that’s transcended the Spice Girls, hasn’t it? You know, it’s out there, even among young generations who may not even know our music or our characters. It’s one of the parts of our legacy we’re so proud of because we empowered so many people, and I meet them all the time. It’s something that’s spoken in our language and printed on T-shirts—I see it when I’m out shopping! I think often, as young people, we can feel powerless or lonely, and [girl power] gave people confidence and courage to go on and feel like they had somewhere to belong. Girl power is something I feel very, very proud of.
See Melanie C at the Showbox, Saturday, September 19, 8:30 pm, 21+

articles.title: Bellevue Council Faces Decision Point on Parking Reform
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Eastside's largest city is grappling with a new state mandate to scale back its off-street parking requirements for new development. In facing choices around going further than the new state-required baseline, Bellevue's leaders are facing crosswinds: a desire to continue reducing barriers to homebuilding is crashing into the city's car-oriented status quo.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

The new mandate is coming thanks to Senate Bill 5184 , a law approved last year that sets strict caps on the number of off-street parking stalls that Washington cities can require with new building projects. By next January, Bellevue will no longer be able to require more than one parking stall for every two apartment units, nor more than two parking stalls for every 1,000 square feet of commercial space.

The City will also be barred from requiring any parking for a broad set of uses, including apartments less than 1,200 square feet in size, commercial spaces that are less than 3,000 square feet, child care facilities, and affordable and senior housing.

The statewide parking reform is intended to ease cost burdens on builders, which are passed along to renters and homebuyers. Adding garage parking typically costs builders $60,000 per stall or more, according to the housing-focused Pacific Northwest think tank Sightline Institute.

Cities across the state are grappling with the new requirements, but Bellevue's size, prevalence of transit infrastructure, and positive trends in housing permit starts are putting a spotlight on how this new mandate gets implemented. Earlier this year, numerous councilmembers expressed clear interest in looking at how to be more ambitious in giving developers flexibility around parking, but recommendations that came out of Bellevue's planning commission hew much closer to the bare minimum.

A growing number of Washington cities are taking steps to fully eliminate parking mandates from their land use codes, following in the footsteps of places like Spokane , Port Townsend , and Bellingham . Vancouver abolished parking mandates as part of its Comprehensive Plan update earlier this year, with Tacoma next on deck. Next door to Bellevue in Issaquah, city leaders are considering eliminating mandates across a wide swath of the center city – an area where increasing housing growth is the goal.

A full repeal is likely a step too far for Bellevue, no matter the studies showing the range of positive benefits that come from doing so. Earlier this year, UCLA's Institute of Transportation Studies published a new research synthesis looking at a range of studies considering the impact of arbitrary requirements to build parking and the quantified benefits that come from wiping them off the books.

"Across the research literature, scholars generally recommend eliminating minimum parking requirements. Removing these mandates lifts a major barrier to new housing and businesses, reduces the risk of parking oversupply, and encourages more efficient use of existing spaces," the researchers noted. "Slowing the growth of parking infrastructure can improve walkability and urban design, reduce environmental harms, and support more sustainable travel behavior."
A full repeal is likely a step too far for Bellevue officials, so instead the debate will focus on pulling a few additional levers.

"Considering that we have appropriately aggressive housing goals, and that many projects are struggling to move forward, I think we should continue to keep our foot on the gas. And I think there are some modifications we should consider to the final code, so that we can do that," Bellevue Deputy Mayor Dave Hamilton said last week.

By 2029, Bellevue will need to remove parking mandates from within a half-mile walk of light rail stations and within a quarter-mile of RapidRide bus stops. The city is going ahead and making that update now, but the council could expand that radius to a half-mile distance from RapidRide stations, which includes the B Line and the K Line , planned to open by 2030.

"Council has already established policy direction that we want more housing capacity near high-capacity transit, including allowing six units by right in a half mile of light rail and quarter mile of bus rapid transit [BRT], removing mandatory parking requirements in those areas that are transit served is consistent with the broader direction," Councilmember Vishal Bhargava said. "I would ask that we consider [...] the half mile around the BRT, and just as an analysis to see what the puts and takes would be towards that."
Naren Briar was the only councilmember to bring up the idea of a full repeal of parking mandates, laying down a potential marker for the future.

"I am personally interested in exploring citywide elimination of parking minimums. According to the research I did, cities like Austin, San Jose, Buffalo, had done this and seen a tremendous amount of economic boost as a result of that. So I do want us to, to be clear, I think if we did that now, it might cause a little bit of chaos," Briar said. "But I do want us eventually to see a city that is comprehensively integrated and allows end-to-end walkability as an effective mode of transportation for senior citizens, for young kids waiting at the bus stop, for for any resident or visitor of Bellevue."

Another issue likely to come up before a final vote in October is visitor parking. The draft code approved by the planning commission includes a set of requirements on top of the minimum required parking stalls for residential units, mandating every development with more than six units include one visitor stall for every 20 units. After 50 units or 20,000 square feet of gross floor area that requirement no longer applies, bizarrely.

"I'm inclined to think that our mandate should be eliminated, and I'm looking to Seattle and Redmond, where they don't have any visitor parking mandate," Hamilton said. "I think housing providers understand their customers' preferences and will build projects accordingly. This may be an area where we can follow the lead of neighboring cities and help ensure that folks who move here are not penalized."

There will also be a push in the other direction. At last Tuesday's meeting, a clear bloc formed in favor of sticking with the planning commission recommendation that included Jared Nieuwenhuis, Lynne Robinson, and Claire Sumadiwirya.

"Myself, I live in a townhouse community, so I would say if there's no visitor parking, somebody is not able to walk a half mile, take the light rail, then nobody's gonna ever visit me," Sumadiwirya said. "I have a lot of elderly friends, so I think it's really important to know that. I appreciate the take of meet the state minimum first. I think whenever there's something [that] changes in the policy, it's always good to be safe and finding that balance versus just I think making drastic, too bold changes that will be different."

Robinson, who served as Bellevue's mayor from 2020 to 2025, went even further than her colleagues and suggested that the city might make a push to amend state law to mandate parking at senior living facilities. She pushed back most strenuously on the idea of going further than the planning commission recommendation.

"Nobody's going to have service providers serve the seniors. Nobody's going to get a visitor, and Silver Glen is our only, I think, our only independent [living facility]," Robinson said. "I guess there's one next to Emerald Court, but independent senior living, and all those people have cars, and most of them cannot walk that far, so they're staying connected to the community by having the ability to drive, and if we take the parking away, it's going to really limit people's ability to live independently."

According to the National Resources Defense Council , 37.6% of Americans over the age of 75 have driving limitations, as of 2025. Nothing in the land use code would limit the ability for developers of senior and independent living facilities from building off-street parking with their projects – removing the mandate simply gets the city out of the business of deciding what's appropriate.
While not likely to represent a major sea change, the October 20 vote on parking reform will certainly signal what direction Bellevue is heading.

articles.title: Link Evening Closure Tuesday-Thursday
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: The downtown tunnel will close early at 11 pm September 15-17 for planned maintenance. This is only in the evenings and won’t affect daytime service. The last Link trains through the tunnel each direction will be:

1 Line shuttle buses will run every 10-15 minutes between Capitol Hill and SODO stations. 2 Line shuttle buses will run every 10-15 minutes between Capitol Hill and Judkins Park stations. An earlier announcement said the shuttle buses would start earlier at 9pm, but Monday’s announcement doesn’t mention this,. so they may or may not start that early.

articles.title: Rob Saka Throws Together Traffic Safety Legislation Ahead of Council Deadline
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle Council transportation committee chair Rob Saka has been rushing forward a set of bills intended to improve traffic safety outcomes on city streets, hoping to beat a legislative deadline before this fall's budget season. The package, which consists of three separate bills , purports to give the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) additional tools to implement safety upgrades, asks for recommendations around timelines to remediate city streets following fatal crashes, and sets the City up to be able to mandate side guards on vehicles used by city contractors.
However, SDOT has confirmed with The Urbanist that the department was not fully looped in on the package's development, with Saka moving things forward on a very compressed timeline.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Saka rolled out his proposal , which he is calling the Seattle SAFER (Safe Accountable Flexible Equitable Responsive) Streets Act, two days before Mayor Katie Wilson signed an executive order that deals with many of the same topics. Saka, due to his role as committee chair, had reportedly received a briefing on the contents of that executive order, but did not appear at Wilson's press event to roll it out in Beacon Hill on August 21.
The overlap between the new executive order and Saka's legislative proposal is particularly pronounced when it comes to potential regulations around side guards and other vehicle safety retrofits.

"I suppose great minds can arrive at some of the same intersections as we appear to have done and aligned on from a legislative and executive perspective, and that's a good thing," Saka said last week, at the second committee meeting held to discuss the bills. "The two efforts are complementary, but distinct. Executive action can move quickly, [and] initiate changes today. Legislation, by comparison, can establish durable requirements that survive changes in administrations, department leadership, or priorities."

When Saka made those comments, all three of the bills remained in draft form, having missed a prior deadline for introduction and referral before the Council's August recess. Holding a committee discussion, much less two, around a draft version of a bill is unusual, and during last week's meeting several issues surfaced that conveyed how rushed the process has been thus far, including the fact that modifications recommended by the City's law department had been made between the August 20 and September 8 meeting.
So what would the SAFER Streets Act actually do?

The first bill in the package adjusts the authority of the SDOT Director, giving that position explicit authority to do many things that are already under their control. That includes the authorization (not requirement) "to ensure capital project reviews are informed by safety needs identified in a Vision Zero Plan when changes to the configuration or operations of an intersection are proposed and when geography and budget allow." It would codify a requirement that the Vision Zero Plan (which appears to be the same as a Vision Zero Action Plan) be updated every three years.

It would also ask SDOT for a report, to be delivered by next June, that considers options for "improving the Department's existing response following a qualifying fatal crash." That work would build on an internal SDOT policy, adopted in May, that codifies expectations around how the department reviews fatal crashes on city right-of-way, with a two to four-week review after SDOT receives a crash report from the Seattle Police Department and a 90-day timeframe for "remediation or maintenance activities."

That internal policy also includes a twice-yearly review of all crashes involving people who were walking, rolling, biking, or using a scooter or motorcycle. That data is used to inform Vision Zero investments with a goal of making safety upgrades within two years of that review.

Saka's bill asks for at least three "progressively more stringent options" for post fatal crash review, including a requirement to evaluate what it would look like to conduct a review within 72 hours of receiving a crash report, and the potential for remediation to take place within two weeks. Presumably this report would be used to inform future legislation, but the bill ultimately doesn't make any direct changes to city policies around post-crash review.

That bill also includes a section dealing with the amount of time that the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) spends reviewing potential modifications to highway on and off-ramps within the city, requesting design feedback be returned "within a reasonable amount of time, but in no case more than 180 days." But the City of Seattle has no legal standing to require any specific timelines from another level of government, turning the section into a pretty please.

The second bill in the package addresses the city position of City Traffic Engineer, a position that has been held by Venu Nemani since 2021. Nemani also holds the title of Chief Transportation Safety Officer, after being "elevated" to that role in 2023 following the release of a "top to bottom" review of the department's Vision Zero program.

The bill would not codify that Chief Transportation Safety Officer position, but rather give the City Traffic Engineer explicit authority to do things that are already commonplace, like the ability to "review and provide recommendations to enhance the safety of roadways and transportation infrastructure." It's not clear that a lack of these specific authorities is inhibiting the department from being able to make safety interventions now, and nothing in the bill would require the City Traffic Engineer to do anything differently.

The third bill, which was only discussed conceptually at the August 20 transportation committee meeting, would request requirements for vehicles operated by city contractors to have "truck lateral protective devices," commonly referred to as truck side guards. Placed along the undercarriage of a vehicle, side guards can prevent people who are walking or rolling from being pulled under the vehicle in the event of a crash.
The bill specifically calls out Boston, which codified truck side guard requirements into city code in 2014, and asks for recommendations by May 1 of next year.

During last week's meeting, members of the council's independent central staff raised issues that came from the Department of Finance and Administrative Services (FAS), which would be tasked with implementing the bill – noting that department wasn't looped in until early September.

"We were able to speak with FAS about this bill last week. Very grateful to them for jumping in and providing their analysis," legislative analyst Ann Gorman said. "They raised a couple issues which we have flagged as policy considerations. FAS may require additional resources to develop the requested recommendations. For instance, FAS does not have mechanical engineering capacity, and FAS may not have capacity to perform and/or oversee the requested body of work by the date that is currently in the ordinance."

Wilson's executive order also directed FAS to work on side guards and other potential safety enhancements for contracted vehicles, but instead asks for a report on opportunities and impacts by next January.

"The executive order is very much in a similar subject area, but it is asking for another thing," Gorman said. "It seems reasonable to expect that after the requested report is delivered [...] the mayor's office might consider developing actual requirements about what it has heard based on the opportunity and impact analysis, but that is not what it is doing."

Other members of the transportation committee, including Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Eddie Lin, have raised concerns about the fact that SDOT has not been at the table at any of the committee meetings so far.

"I would be interested in hearing SDOT's feedback, and just want to make sure that – not that we have to adopt what they say – but I do just want to make sure that this is going to work for them as well, and if there are potential concerns or tweaking of anything, that I'd like to have the time to bring those forward for discussion," Lin said.

SDOT press secretary Ethan Bergerson confirmed via email late last week that the department was only looped in on Saka's package on August 19, the day before the first committee discussion was held. SDOT did provide feedback on the bill on September 4, Bergerson said, but no changes were incorporated by the September 8 meeting when Saka assured his colleagues that no further changes would be made. The Urbanist has not yet confirmed the substance of SDOT's feedback.

Councilmembers raised other process concerns. Because the bills aren't set to be formally introduced until September 15, two days before a final committee vote, the deadline to submit amendments was last week. That means councilmembers will have not seen a final version of the bill when being asked to submit potential changes.
"I've never seen an amendment deadline for a piece of legislation that has not formally been introduced yet. How is that possible?" Rinck, the committee's vice chair, asked staff last week.
"I can only tell you that we've been working out how to make all of the pieces fit, and this is the timeline that we've developed to achieve this vote date," was the reply from analyst Amanda Allen.

Saka defended the process to develop the package, and the fact that SDOT has not been at the table for committee discussions, stating that it is common for departments to not be directly involved in meetings on proposals that originate from the legislative branch.

"My office has been working closely with SDOT on this, especially [over] the last six weeks plus, even before that, on various higher-level aspects of this," Saka said. "They have reviewed and provided my office with extensive feedback, and my office has met directly with the department, and the executive, the mayor's office, on our complimentary efforts numerous times. And I would encourage you, Councilmember Lin, vice chair [Rinck] as well, anyone, to meet directly with the department yourselves."

A final committee vote is tentatively scheduled for this Thursday, September 17. If that vote isn't taken, the package would likely be held until the council wraps up its budget work around Thanksgiving.

articles.title: “Hop On Board!” Campaign Kicks Off
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: Yesterday, a coalition of transit advocates launched “Hop On Board!”, the official campaign urging Seattle voters to pass the renewal and expansion of the Seattle Transit Measure this November . Speakers at the event included Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck, ATU 587 President Greg Woodfill, Nondrivers Alliance founder Anna Zivarts, Transit Riders Union General Manager Lam Ho, and Transportation Choices Coalition ‘s Executive Director Kirk Hovenkotter and Policy Director Katy Ricchiuto.

The Transportation Choices Coalition is leading local advocates pushing for expansion of the transit measure, which proposes to increase the current 0.15% sales tax for transit to 0.3%, the maximum allowed under recently adopted state law. If approved by voters, the measure would take effect in April 2027.

King County Metro uses an equity framework to distribute service across King County but cities have the ability to purchase additional service. Seattle has been buying additional service since 2014 , which brought frequent buses to most of the city and dramatically increased the viability of living car-free.

The current Seattle Transit Measure funds over 7% of all bus trips currently running in Seattle, mainly boosting service along key corridors during the day and providing the majority of Metro’s Night Owl service in the city. The expanded STM would further boost service at night and on weekends, as well as more than doubling the number of free ORCA cards for those who need it and providing funding for several important accessibility programs. The measure also includes funding for capital funding for bus lanes.

At the event, speakers shared stories of how important transit is to their lives and how this measure would make public transit in Seattle more useful for more people. Mayor Wilson focused on the importance of late night bus service to help service workers get home at the end of a late shift without using a rideshare service like Uber or Lyft, or making it possible for a family with two cars to only need one.

Councilmember Rinck shared stories of three-seat rides to Tumwater and the importance of frequent, reliable service, and also highlighted the expanded late night service provided by the measure. Greg Woodfill posited that although sales taxes are regressive, this measure’s taxes will go right back to serving the people who need it most, stating “every $1 spent on transit is $5 back in the community”. Anna Zivarts stressed the importantance of frequent and reliable service to those who cannot drive, and how the transit measure would bring more service to more communities. Zivarts put it simply: “transit is freedom”. Other speakers highlighted the proposed increase in free ORCA passes for low-income riders and the elderly, and the importance of pushing back against likely opposition to the measure.
If you are intersested in supporting the Hop On Board campaign, you can sign up to volunteer for upcoming events , or donate to the campaign .

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: New Speed Cameras
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On Wednesday, SDOT announced four new speed cameras will be installed across Seattle in 2027. These four cameras are the first of 10 cameras that will be installed by March 2029, per Mayor Wilson’s Vision Zero executive order . The selected locations were chosen as they are some of the most dangerous sections of Seattle’s road network. Speed cameras cannot replace full road redesigns, but they are an effective temporary measure until a concrete redesign is implemented. The four cameras will be installed at:

These broad sections will be narrowed down to the exact camera locations over the next few months. Signs warning drivers of the cameras will be installed 30 days before the cameras are turned on. Once the cameras are enabled, they will only issue warnings for the first 30 days.

The four locations chosen for this initial batch of speed cameras are hotspots for dangerous driving. SDOT data show these sections have an 85th percentile speed more than 10mph above the speed limit. While a 5mph or 10mph difference may be insignificant to a driver, faster speeds are much more deadly. A 2011 study found that someone has a 70% higher chance of being killed by a vehicle traveling at 30mph versus at 25mph. Over the last three years, the four sections have collectively had 305 crashes that caused 138 injuries and 3 fatalities.

The four new cameras will join a growing network of red light cameras, school speed safety cameras, block the box cameras, and bus lane cameras. These cameras are not used for any purposes other than traffic safety. From SDOT: “State law requires that traffic safety cameras may only film when they detect a traffic violation. The video cannot be used as evidence to prosecute other kinds of crimes aside from speeding.”

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.
